extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy / Plato (undergraduate or general readers interested in political/ethical theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Close commentary and exposition of Book IV–V of Plato's Republic, explicating the account of the four cardinal virtues, the tripartite soul, political arrangements (guardians, communal property, mating), and methodological points about defining faculties and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of the 'greatest happiness' principle
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The greatest happiness’ principle is not the true foundation of ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains multiple ambiguities of 'happiness' (pleasure vs ideal life, subjective vs objective, worldly vs otherworldly, self vs all), that it lacks the definiteness and moral appeal of 'truth' and 'right', and is too associated with comforts rather than 'the goods of the soul'. Concludes that while a utilitarian notion may be a useful secondary principle (often easier of application), it cannot serve as first principle of ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political expediency vs. right/truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Political measures are chiefly asked: How will they affect the happiness of mankind? but expediency is merely the law of right limited by human social conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues right and truth remain the highest aims of government; they appeal to the better mind of nations and should not be abandoned because they cannot be directly enforced. Even in utilitarian states the power of ideas and idealism among statesmen persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception of the whole as foundation of politics and art
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'whole' lies at the foundation both of politics and of art, supplying the principle of criticism (harmony, symmetry, measure, proportion, unity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conception underpins judgments about political organization and aesthetic evaluation; used to argue for unity and order in the State and in works of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: State limited in size (Greek model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The State should be limited in size, following the traditional model of a Greek city (Hellas), where smallness of cities is converted into a principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a requirement to make government practicable and to sustain the moral/educational regime; implicit comparison with Aristotle's Politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour / every one doing his own business
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice (in the State and individual) can be defined as 'every one having his own' — that is, each person doing his own business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a central political principle to prevent role-confusion (e.g., a cobbler becoming a guardian). Practical allowances: while carpenters may cobble occasionally, grave evil arises when a single individual unites incompatible roles (trainer, warrior, legislator). This division is tested further by mapping onto parts of the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four cardinal virtues present in the perfect State
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfect State will contain all four virtues—wisdom, courage, temperance, justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates orders the analysis by eliminating three virtues to reveal justice as the remaining notion; the virtues correspond to classes in the State and parts of the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom as the skill of the guardians (politic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom is the skill of him who advises about the interests of the whole State—the skill concentrated in the guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not the craft of artisans but political prudence; if the ruling (small) class possesses this wisdom, the whole State will be wise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage defined as preservation of right opinion about dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is 'the never-failing salvation of the opinions which law and education have prescribed concerning dangers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by analogy of dye fixed on a properly prepared ground: education (ground) plus law (colour) fixes right opinion so that neither pleasure nor pain washes it out; labelled 'political' or 'civilized' courage to distinguish from animal courage or higher intellectual courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance as harmony/mastery of self
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance suggests harmony and is described by the popular phrase 'master of himself'—the better principle mastering the worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance is a harmony diffused through all classes, making citizens 'of one mind' and attuning the different classes like strings of an instrument; it belongs to both rulers and subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as universal order: each doing his own business
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the perfect order by which all natures and classes do their own business; the right man in the right place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice is more abstract and universal than the other virtues and is the foundation (from Plato's point of view) to which the others are referred; injustice is the insubordination of inferior elements and is harmful like disease to the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of residues to define justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates uses a method of residues: eliminate wisdom, courage, temperance from the State and see what remains—this remainder is justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method is characterized as simple and 'obvious'; indicates an approach of defining a concept by subtracting other known virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite soul: rational, irascible (spirit), concupiscent (desire)
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual soul is divided into three parts—reason, spirit (irascible/passions), and desire/concupiscence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part corresponds to a class in the State; reason corresponds to rulers, spirit to warriors, desire to producers. The division justifies mapping virtues of the State to virtues of the individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for distinguishing faculties: different workings (no contradictory effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculties are distinguished by difference in their working: the same faculty cannot produce contradictory effects at the same time in the same relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples use thirst and reason (thirst urging drink vs rational restraint) and the Leontius anecdote to motivate positing distinct principles; warns about modified terms (e.g., 'angry thirst') which can blur distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion (spirit) as ally of reason and foundation of courage
rubrics_metrics.description: The irascible faculty (passion/spirit) is often found aiding reason against desire; it is the ally of reason and the foundation of courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion exists in children and brutes and can be aroused by righteous indignation; it differs from anger because of an affinity to reason; Plato's usage of these terms shifts in later works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of State virtues and individual virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtues of the State and the individual are the same: wisdom, courage, temperance, justice in the State are respectively wisdom, courage, temperance, justice in the individuals composing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just state and just individual avoid theft, lying, adultery, impiety; justice binds the three chords of the soul and acts harmoniously in every relation of life; education (music and gymnastic) harmonizes faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as health and beauty of the soul; vice as disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is the health, beauty, and well-being of the soul; vice is the disease, weakness, and deformity of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral education and right acts produce good habits as healthy practices produce health; injustice produces inharmonious disorder analogous to bodily disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four forms of vice and corresponding state/soul types
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four forms of vice or decline in states and corresponding soul-types; the single form of virtue corresponds to a particular just state where reason rules (monarchy/aristocracy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches typology of five forms of states and souls (implied: timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, tyranny etc.), locating the just polity among them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education (music and gymnastic) as means to harmonize parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and gymnastic (broadly, cultural and physical education) are used to harmonize the rational, spirited, and desirous parts of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education lays the 'ground' so that the 'dye' of laws fixes right opinions; proper education ensures that neither pleasure nor pain will wash out right opinions about dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and character of guardians: watch-dogs of the State
rubrics_metrics.description: The guardians of the State are to be 'watch-dogs'—a small class concentrated with the wisdom and policy of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians are selected, trained, and expected to enforce laws and make new ones; they receive special education and live under strict social arrangements to ensure loyalty and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women: equal employments if the same education and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: If women have the same aptitudes, they should share the same employments and receive the same education (music, gymnastics, art of war) as men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues sex-differences are often partial and accidental; where capacities are shared, education must be the same to train the best women as guardians and soldiers; anticipates social ridicule but appeals to habit and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communism of wives, children, and property for unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposes community of wives, children, and common property among the guardians to create unity and prevent private interests from causing discord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues common meals, common houses, and shared child-rearing produce identity of interest; claims private property and familial ties breed strife; permits regulated festivals and enforced mating to maintain population and social harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers' use of 'noble falsehoods' and strict selection of mating
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers must sometimes use a strong dose of falsehood to bring about desirable unions and to maintain social order; they will pair the good with the good, and the bad with the bad (selective mating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes orchestration of hymeneal festivals, use of lots to conceal rulers' interventions, and the practice of attributing engineered pairings to chance to maintain cohesion and population quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eugenic measures: rearing of offspring and destruction of inferior infants
rubrics_metrics.description: Offspring of the brave and fair will be reared in an enclosure; the rest will be 'hurried away to places unknown'—a means of preserving the flock in prime condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nurses attend children, mothers may not recognize their own offspring, and attendants handle nighttime care; suggestion of destroying inferior offspring is presented as part of social engineering for the State's benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of ages and marriages for procreation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents should be in the prime of life for procreation (men roughly 25–55, women 20–40); participating outside specified ages or forming marriage connections without rulers' consent is impiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies age ranges and the institutionalization of mating festivals; addresses questions about kinship recognition under communal arrangements and defines degrees of affinity by timing of births after espousals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the State as the highest good; elimination of private pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest good of a State is unity; the greatest evil is discord and distraction—unity is achieved where there are no private pleasures or property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues common property produces common pleasures and pains and reduces flattery, household cares, and lawsuits; citizens become tightly bound, sharing in joys and sufferings of the State as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military training of youth by observation and veterans
rubrics_metrics.description: Young warriors must learn by looking on (observation) and being trained by experienced veterans, including riding instruction and appropriate graduated risk-taking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares to craftsmen's apprenticeships (potters' boys); cowards and deserters are degraded to lower classes; heroism is rewarded with honors and special social privileges (more wives, better food, public honours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Honouring and rewarding bravery
rubrics_metrics.description: Bravery is honoured publicly: crown by youths, right hand of fellowship, kissing, more wives, more food at feasts, and posthumous worship as guardian angels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides concrete social rewards and ritual honouring (civic coronation, feasting privileges, cultic honours after death) to incentivize military virtue and breeding of brave families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of enemies as a policy question
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether Hellenes (fellow Greeks) shall be enslaved; answer given: No, because of risk to the whole race passing under the yoke of barbarians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gestures to international/political prudence and long-term consequences of enslavement policy; places limits on wartime conduct as guided by concern for the species/nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion: base on highest conception of gods and maintain Hellenic type
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion should be based on the highest conception of the gods and the true national or Hellenic type should be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religion is treated lightly in the exposition but is included as one of two great principles the State must provide for; its cultivation supports national character and moral education.
